preamble: Denasalization of [ũ] to oral [u]. In Galician-Portuguese, loss of intervocalic n left a nasal vowel that was later denasalized (Latin lūna > lũa > Portuguese lua, Galician lúa). In Germanic, the nasal vowels left by loss of n before a fricative were denasalized: late Proto-Germanic *ų̄ from *-unh- gave Gothic ū, and the Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law gave Old English ūs 'us'. In Lithuanian, the nasal vowel written ų became long [uː] in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.

examples.note: Galician has the cognate lúa; lũa survives as an archaic or dialectal form.
Old Icelandic still had a nasal vowel in ǿ̇ra, as recorded in the First Grammatical Treatise.
Old Frisian also has ūs; compare German uns.
The ogonek now marks only length.
